title: Alternating series and their error estimates
terms: alternating series; Leibniz alternating-series test; alternating remainder bound; eventual monotonicity.

If b ≥ 0, b decreases eventually, and b → 0, then (−1) b converges. All three ingredi-
n n n n
ents matter: alternating signs alone do not imply convergence, and a zero term limit without
suitable control does not suffice. A finite exceptional beginning does not affect convergence.
When the decrease holds from the start, the error after N terms has magnitude at most b
N+1
and the sign of the first omitted term. Thus consecutive partial sums bracket the sum. This
often gives a simpler approximation guarantee than Taylor’s derivative remainder. If the term
magnitudes fail to decrease, look for absolute convergence or another argument rather than
applying this test automatically.
If monotonicity begins only later, apply the remainder theorem to the omitted tail once that
tail is decreasing to zero. The finitely many earlier irregular magnitudes do not affect this tail
estimate. Alternating signs and terms tending to zero alone are insufficient.

The magnitudes decrease strictly to zero. Even partial sums omit a positive next term and

decrease makes the displayed inequalities strict.

How does [(−1) / n + 1/n] behave?
n=1
(A) It converges absolutely.
(B) It converges conditionally.
(C) It diverges to +∞.
(D) It diverges to −∞.
(E) Its partial sums remain bounded but fail to converge.

solution.text:
The partial sums are the sum of a convergent alternating square-root series and the diver-
gent harmonic partial sums, so they tend to +∞. Yet the individual terms tend to zero
and, apart from any initial exception, alternate in sign. Their magnitudes do not satisfy
the necessary monotonic control for the alternating-series test.
